{{draft}} '''{{Ill|{{PAGENAME}}|ja|海神神社|simple}}''' (海神神社) is a significant Shinto shrine located in [[Tsushima Island]], Nagasaki that holds a [[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo status]]. This status denotes that the shrine is remarkable and holds a significant historical importance. Kaijin Shrine is also ranked as an [[Ichinomiya]], which means it is the highest-ranked shrine in its province.
Kaijin Shrine should not be confused with {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|simple}}, which has a very similar Japanese name (海神社) to Kaijin Shrine (海神神社).
In 2012 a robber stole a Buddha statue from the shrine, but in 2015 it was returned.<ref>{{Cite web |title=South Korea Returns Stolen Buddhist Statue to Japan {{!}} Buddhistdoor |url=https://www2.buddhistdoor.net/news/south-korea-returns-stolen-buddhist-statue-to-japan |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=www2.buddhistdoor.net}}</ref>

Kaijin Shrine is also ranked as an [[Ichinomiya]], which means it is the highest-ranked shrine in its province.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Mine Town |url=http://tsushima.weebly.com/mine-town.html |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Tsushima Island |language=en}}</ref>

[[Ghost of Tsushima]] fans helped raise money to repair it.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-01-12 |title=Ghost of Tsushima fans come together to help fund repair of Watatsumi Shrine gate |url=https://www.destructoid.com/ghost-of-tsushima-fans-come-together-to-help-fund-repair-of-watatsumi-shrine-gate/ |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=Destructoid |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}}</ref>
The Kaijin Shrine on Tsushima Island holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers.<ref name=":1" />
These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location.<ref name=":1" />
One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe.<ref name=":1" />
Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami.<ref name=":1" />

== Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}}</ref>
The Kaijin Shrine on Tsushima Island holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers.<ref name=":1" />
These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location.<ref name=":1" />
One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe.<ref name=":1" />
Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami.<ref name=":1" />

'''{{ill|Kaijin Shrine|ja| 海神神社|zh| 海神神社|simple}}''' (海神神社) also read as Watatsumi Shrine is a significant Shinto shrine located in [[Tsushima Island]], Nagasaki that holds a [[Beppyo shrine|Beppyo status]]. This status denotes that the shrine is remarkable and holds a significant historical importance. Kaijin Shrine is also ranked as an [[Ichinomiya]], which means it is the highest-ranked shrine in its province.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Mine Town |url=http://tsushima.weebly.com/mine-town.html |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Tsushima Island |language=en}}</ref> It is located near Mount Izu.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yCpQAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22 |title=Proceedings |date=2006 |publisher=Architectural Institute of Korea |language=en}}</ref>
[[Empress Jingu]] visited the area to worship at Mount Izu.<ref name=":0" />
'''[[ja:海神神社]]'''
Kaijin Shrine should not be confused with {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}}, which has a very similar Japanese name (海神社) to Kaijin Shrine (海神神社).
It has a Bronze [[Buddha statue]] from Korea in it.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lWLrAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22 |title=Archives of Asian Art |date=1987 |publisher=Asia Society |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lf0KAQAAMAAJ&q=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22 |title=Japan Close-up |date=2007 |publisher=PHP International |language=en}}</ref> The statue is designated as important cultural property.<ref name=":2" />
In 2012 a robber stole a Silla era Buddha statue from the shrine<ref name="www2buddhistdoornet-2023a" />, on the same day they stole another statue from [[Kannon-ji]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hae-yeon |first=Kim |date=2023-10-26 |title=Supreme Court dismisses Buseoksa's appeal in Bodhisattva statue ownership dispute |url=https://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20231026000667 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=The Korea Herald |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hae-yeon |first=Kim |date=2023-02-06 |title=Buseoksa to appeal court ruling on Bodhisattva statue stolen from Japan |url=https://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20230206000649 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=The Korea Herald |language=en}}</ref> but in 2015 it was returned.<ref name="www2buddhistdoornet-2023a">{{Cite web |title=South Korea Returns Stolen Buddhist Statue to Japan {{!}} Buddhistdoor |url=https://www2.buddhistdoor.net/news/south-korea-returns-stolen-buddhist-statue-to-japan |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=www2.buddhistdoor.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Press |first=Jiji |date=2023-02-02 |title=S. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}}</ref>
The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers.<ref name=":1" />
These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location.<ref name=":1" />
One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe.<ref name=":1" />
Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami.<ref name=":1" />

The game's shrine is dedicated to Tsukuyomi. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There is a legal dispute over who owns it. Buseok Temple in Seosan claims to own it. Evidence suggests the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. Experts think Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The statue will stay in South Korea until the dispute is resolved. If Buseok Temple cannot prove the statue was illegally taken from Korea, it will be sent back to Japan. The issue of Korean artifacts in Japan is sensitive. Many were taken illegally. Korean Court Denies Temple's Ownership of Statue Stolen from Japan |url=https://japannews.yomiuri.co.jp/society/general-news/20230202-88365/ |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=japannews.yomiuri.co.jp |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2015-05-27 |title=S. Korea court rejects suit seeking return of statue to Japan {{!}} GlobalPost |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527150211/http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/kyodo-news-international/140502/s-korea-court-rejects-suit-seeking-return-statue-japan |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=web.archive.org}}{{Cite web |date=2015-05-27 |title=S. Korea court rejects suit seeking return of statue to Japan {{!}} GlobalPost |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527150211/http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/kyodo-news-international/140502/s-korea-court-rejects-suit-seeking-return-statue-japan |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=web.archive.org}} [[File:海神神社の空中写真.jpg|thumb|Shrine area]] [[Ghost of Tsushima]] fans helped raise money to repair it.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Ghost of Tsushima fans have helped raise $260k for repairs on the real island |url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/ghost-of-tsushima-fans-have-helped-raise-260k-for-repairs-on-the-real-island/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=VGC |language=en-GB}}{{Cite web |date=2021-01-12 |title=Ghost of Tsushima fans come together to help fund repair of Watatsumi Shrine gate |url=https://www.destructoid.com/ghost-of-tsushima-fans-come-together-to-help-fund-repair-of-watatsumi-shrine-gate/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Destructoid |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Oloman |first=Jordan |date=2021-01-11 |title=Ghost of Tsushima Fans Help With Real-Life Tsushima Island Repairs |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/ghost-of-tsushima-fans-help-with-real-life-tsushima-island-repairs |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=IGN |language=en}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == The Watatsumi Shrine is in the Toyotama region of Tsushima. In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to Tsukuyomi. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[:Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[:Category:Ichinomiya]] [[:Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[:Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[:Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[:Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[:Category:Tsushima]] [[:Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }}

|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/ghost-of-tsushima-fans-help-with-real-life-tsushima-island-repairs |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=IGN |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Kaijin Shrine Tathagata Buddha |url=https://research.cgu.edu/cultural-property-disputes-resource/cpdr/kaijin-shrine-tathagata-buddha |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Cultural Property Disputes Resource |language=en-US}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. The head priest's name is Negitama. He mentioned problems with tourists on Twitter. He said foreign tourists had picnics at the shrine. The shrine is on Tsushima Island in Nagasaki Prefecture. A YouTuber filmed there without permission. Tour guides did not respect the shrine's sacred areas. They stood on the steps of shrine buildings. Korean graffiti was found on a board for prayer plaques. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == The Watatsumi Shrine is in the Toyotama region of Tsushima. In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to Tsukuyomi. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[:Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[:Category:Ichinomiya]] [[:Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[:Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[:Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[:Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[:Category:Tsushima]] [[:Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }}

|url=https://research.cgu.edu/cultural-property-disputes-resource/cpdr/kaijin-shrine-tathagata-buddha |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Cultural Property Disputes Resource |language=en-US}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]]. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[:Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[:Category:Ichinomiya]] [[:Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[:Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[:Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[:Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[:Category:Tsushima]] [[:Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }}

== Kaijin Shrine is a significant shrine on Tsushima Island. It is known as the "Shrine of the Sea Kami." This shrine was the most important one in the past. It was called ichi no miya. The shrine was originally linked to the sea deity Watatsumi. Later, it became associated with Hachiman. This association is mentioned in late Heian period sources.{{Rp|page=98}} The shrine's founding story involves Empress Jingū. She placed eight banners at the shrine after returning from Korea. These banners are why the shrine is connected to Hachiman. Hachiman means "Eight Banners." This led to another name for the shrine, "Hachiman Hongū." This name means "original shrine of Hachiman." This story is a local tradition. It is not confirmed by other Hachiman chronicles.{{Rp|page=98}} [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane]] argues that Hachiman may have entered Japan through this shrine, as a Buddhist deity from Korea, and that this predated the association with [[Emperor Ōjin|Emperor Ōjin.]]{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. |url=https://research.cgu.edu/cultural-property-disputes-resource/cpdr/kaijin-shrine-tathagata-buddha |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Cultural Property Disputes Resource |language=en-US}} == History == Kaijin Shrine is a significant shrine on Tsushima Island. It is known as the "Shrine of the Sea Kami." This shrine was the most important one in the past. It was called ichi no miya. The shrine was originally linked to the sea deity Watatsumi. Later, it became associated with Hachiman. This association is mentioned in late Heian period sources.{{Rp|page=98}} The shrine's founding story involves Empress Jingū. She placed eight banners at the shrine after returning from Korea. These banners are why the shrine is connected to Hachiman. Hachiman means "Eight Banners." This led to another name for the shrine, "Hachiman Hongū." This name means "original shrine of Hachiman." This story is a local tradition. It is not confirmed by other Hachiman chronicles.{{Rp|page=98}} [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane]] argues that Hachiman may have entered Japan through this shrine, as a Buddhist deity from Korea, and that this predated the association with [[Emperor Ōjin|Emperor Ōjin.]]{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. Medieval sources considered Kaijin Shrine as the origin of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman-gū]] in Kyoto.{{Rp|page=98}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]]. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[Category:Tsushima]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }} {{Hachiman Faith}}

Architecture == == History == Kaijin Shrine is a significant shrine on Tsushima Island. It is known as the "Shrine of the Sea Kami." This shrine was the most important one in the past. It was called ichi no miya. The shrine was originally linked to the sea deity Watatsumi. Later, it became associated with Hachiman. This association is mentioned in late Heian period sources.{{Rp|page=98}} The shrine's founding story involves Empress Jingū. She placed eight banners at the shrine after returning from Korea. These banners are why the shrine is connected to Hachiman. Hachiman means "Eight Banners." This led to another name for the shrine, "Hachiman Hongū." This name means "original shrine of Hachiman." This story is a local tradition. It is not confirmed by other Hachiman chronicles.{{Rp|page=98}} [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane]] argues that Hachiman may have entered Japan through this shrine, as a Buddhist deity from Korea, and that this predated the association with [[Emperor Ōjin|Emperor Ōjin.]]{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. Medieval sources considered Kaijin Shrine as the origin of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman-gū]] in Kyoto.{{Rp|page=98}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. Medieval sources considered Kaijin Shrine as the origin of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman-gū]] in Kyoto.{{Rp|page=98}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]]. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{Cite web |title=Why Was Umisachibiko Attacked? |url=https://www.kokugakuin.ac.jp/en/article/101683 |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=國學院大學 |language=en}}{{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[Category:Tsushima]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }} {{Hachiman Faith}}

Architecture == == History == Kaijin Shrine is a significant shrine on Tsushima Island. It is known as the "Shrine of the Sea Kami." This shrine was the most important one in the past. It was called ichi no miya. The shrine was originally linked to the sea deity [[Watatsumi]]. Later, it became associated with Hachiman. This association is mentioned in late Heian period sources.{{Rp|page=98}} The shrine's founding story involves Empress Jingū. She placed eight banners at the shrine after returning from Korea. These banners are why the shrine is connected to Hachiman. Hachiman means "Eight Banners." This led to another name for the shrine, "Hachiman Hongū." This name means "original shrine of Hachiman." This story is a local tradition. It is not confirmed by other Hachiman chronicles.{{Rp|page=98}} [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane]] argues that Hachiman may have entered Japan through this shrine, as a Buddhist deity from Korea, and that this predated the association with [[Emperor Ōjin|Emperor Ōjin.]]{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. Medieval sources considered Kaijin Shrine as the origin of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman-gū]] in Kyoto.{{Rp|page=98}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]]. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{Cite web |title=Why Was Umisachibiko Attacked? |url=https://www.kokugakuin.ac.jp/en/article/101683 |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=國學院大學 |language=en}}{{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[Category:Tsushima]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }} {{Hachiman Faith}}

== Kaijin Shrine is a significant shrine on Tsushima Island. It is known as the "Shrine of the Sea Kami." This shrine was the most important one in the past. It was called the [[ichinomiya]]. The shrine was originally linked to the sea deity [[Watatsumi]]. Later, it became associated with Hachiman. This association is mentioned in late Heian period sources.{{Rp|page=98}} The shrine's founding story involves Empress Jingū. She placed eight banners at the shrine after returning from Korea. These banners are why the shrine is connected to Hachiman. Hachiman means "Eight Banners." This led to another name for the shrine, "Hachiman Hongū." This name means "original shrine of Hachiman." This story is a local tradition. It is not confirmed by other Hachiman chronicles.{{Rp|page=98}} [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane]] argues that Hachiman may have entered Japan through this shrine, as a Buddhist deity from Korea, and that this predated the association with [[Emperor Ōjin|Emperor Ōjin.]]{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=}}[[Emperor Ōjin|{{Rp|page=44}}]] It is postulated that Hachiman may have been more linked to [[Empress Jingū]] in the early days of the Hachiman faith rather than her son [[Emperor Ojin]].{{Rp|page=97-99}} This has parallels with [[Shikaumi Shrine]] which is a Hachiman shrine that strongly worships [[Empress Jingū]] and whose myths primarily revolve around Jingu's activities while pregnant with Ojin and invading the [[Samhan|Three Han]].{{rp|xxvii}} On Iki Island, Hachiman shrines are omnipresent. The Seven Shrines of Iki pilgrimage route is led by the Shōmo-gū. This shrine is dedicated to Empress Jingū. Three other shrines on the route are also dedicated to Hachiman..{{Rp|page=97-99}} On Hirado Island, Shijiki Shrine is the oldest and most prestigious. It is dedicated to the mythical figure Tokiwake. He was a general in Empress Jingū's military campaign..{{Rp|page=97-99}} Empress Jingū is more central to Hachiman worship on these islands than her son Ōjin. This is clear from various legends. One such story is in the Zenrin kokuhōki. It tells of Zen master Enni Ben’en encountering a storm. A woman appeared on his ship, claiming to be Hachiman Daibosatsu. She protected the ship..{{Rp|page=97-99}} Another legend is from the Ōei Invasion of 1419. It involves a fabricated story of a sea battle victory. The story mentions a powerful female leader. This figure resembles Empress Jingū. In the story, she drowns enemies herself. This mirrors another scene from Jingū's legend..{{Rp|page=97-99}} In these legends, Empress Jingū is depicted differently from traditional Hachiman iconography. Traditional images focus on male figures. These include Emperor Ōjin and the Great Boddhisattva Hachiman. The focus on Jingū suggests a unique interpretation of Hachiman worship in these areas. This might be influenced by beliefs during the wakō period..{{Rp|page=97-99}} There is also a "new" Hachiman shrine in the southern part of Tsushima. Medieval sources considered Kaijin Shrine as the origin of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Hachiman-gū]] in Kyoto.{{Rp|page=98}} It and many other Hachiman shrines of the region switched their deities of worship during the [[Meiji Restoration]].{{Rp|page=98}} == Statue theft == A bronze statue of the Tathagata Buddha has been returned to Tsushima, Japan. It is one of two Buddhist statues stolen three years ago. These statues are important cultural properties of Japan. In October 2012, thieves from South Korea stole the statues. The theft happened in Tsushima. The stolen items included an 8th-century bronze Buddha and a 14th-century Avalokiteshvara. Four people involved in the theft were arrested in South Korea. They tried to sell the statues. They were sentenced to prison in 2013. Japan asked for the statues back many times. South Korea kept them at the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage. There were claims that Japan might have stolen them from Korea. Later, South Korea found no evidence that the Buddha statue was illegally taken to Japan. They decided to return it to Japan. The Tathagata Buddha statue was returned to the Kaijin Shrine shrine. It was reported to be slightly chipped. The time of the damage is unknown. Buseoksa Temple in South Korea claimed the Avalokiteshvara statue. They said it was stolen from them by Japanese pirates. They filed a legal case to stop its return to Japan. They argued that evidence said the statue was made at the temple in the 1330s. They argued Japanese pirates might have looted it in the late Goryeo period. The stayed in South Korea until the dispute was resolved. The Daejeon District Court first supported Buseoksa Temple in 2017. They cited historical evidence of Japan taking the statue. But the Daejeon High Court later disagreed. They said Kannonji Temple in Japan legally owned the statue. The temple said they got the statue in a trade in 1527. The Supreme Court's decision supported the High Court. It said there is no proof linking the old Goryeo temple to today's Buseoksa in Seosan. The decision was based on Japanese law. This law says ownership can be gained if someone has an item for over 20 years. Kannonji Temple had been a legal entity since January 1953. So the statue was returned. == Tourist issues == In January 2020 they banned foreigners due to behavioral issues by [[South Korea|South Korean]] guests. The ban was due to vandalism, thefts, and a threat against the head priest. Complaints included picnics at the shrine, a YouTuber filming there without permission, toour guides disrespecting sacred areas, and Korean graffiti. Some amulets were stolen. A Korean tour guide threatened the priest's life. This ban substantially reduced the amount of Korean tourists who visited [[Tsushima Island|Tsushima]]. == Typhoon destruction == A typhoon damaged the Torii gate at Watatsumi Shrine in Tsushima, Japan. This happened in September 2020. A crowdfunding campaign started on November 27, 2020 on the Japanese website Camp-Fire. It aimed to repair the gate.{{Cite web |date=2021-01-11 |title=Tsushima's Watatsumi Shrine Crowdfunding Ended at Over 500% |url=https://www.siliconera.com/tsushimas-watatsumi-shrine-crowdfunding-ended-at-over-500/ |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=Siliconera |language=en-US}} The campaign reached its initial goal quickly. This goal was 5 million yen. It was reached by December 1, 2020. The campaign ended on January 10, 2021. It raised 27,103,882 yen. This is about $260,435. Many donors were fans of the "[[Ghost of Tsushima]]" game. The restoration was planned to start in April 2021,, and to finish by August 2021. There were plans for a stone monument. It would list the names of those who donated at least 10,000 yen. Concerns were raised over coronavirus affecting the construction. == In popular culture == In the game "Ghost of Tsushima," there is a similar shrine. It is the Scarlet Rock Shrine. The real shrine is dedicated to two deities, [[Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] and [[Toyotama-hime|Toyotamabime]]. The game's shrine is dedicated to [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]]. == Kaijin Matsuri == Kaijin Matsuri is a Shinto festival in Japan. It honors sea gods, fishermen, and naval warfare. The festival happens in the summer. It is held at shrines along the coast.{{Cite book |last=Publishing |first=Bloomsbury |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk7eEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kaijin+Shrine%22&pg=PA489 |title=Religious Celebrations [2 volumes]: An Encyclopedia of Holidays, Festivals, Solemn Observances, and Spiritual Commemorations [2 volumes] |date=2011-09-13 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-1-59884-206-7 |language=en}} The Kaijin Shrine on [[Tsushima Island]] holds a typical festival. It takes place every September. The festival starts with music and dance. Participants wear black and white. They form a procession. Men with lances and shields lead it. They carry three portable shrines from the temple to the beach. A priest performs the kaijin ritual there. The ritual includes casting shellfish into the sea. This is to wish for a good catch for fishermen. It also supports the island's farmers. These festivals are different from fall harvest festivals. Each shrine has its own annual celebrations. These depend on the shrine's location. One major shrine for Kaijin Matsuri is Sumiyoshi Shrine in Osaka. This shrine is important for the festival. It leads many other shrines. These shrines worship the Sumiyoshi kami. These deities are linked to Orion's three main stars. These stars were used for ancient ship navigation. The head temple is in Osaka. It was built in the third century. There are older Sumiyoshi temples in Fukuoka, Iki, and Kobe. Another deity worshiped at these festivals is Suijin. Suijin is also known as Mizu no Kamisama or the Water Kami. Suijin protects fishermen. She is also a patron of fertility, motherhood, and childbirth. Suiten-gu shrines across Japan worship her. Stone markers for her are found even inland. The main shrine for Suijin is in Kurume, Fukuoka. Suijin is believed to come from Ame no Minakanushi. This deity is the ancestor of all Japanese kami. == See Also == * {{Ill|Watatsumi Shrine|lt=Watatsumi Shrine|simple|4=Draft}} [[zh:海神神社]] == References == {{Cite web |title=Why Was Umisachibiko Attacked? |url=https://www.kokugakuin.ac.jp/en/article/101683 |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=國學院大學 |language=en}}{{reflist}} == External links == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=Vq5PZA0nv2Q The festival of Kaijin Shrine in Tsushima, Japan] {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagasaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Temples and shrines that suffered cultural property theft]] [[Category:Tsushima]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Tsushima, Aichi]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] }} {{Hachiman Faith}}
